draft.title: Thomson and the electron
card: A cathode ray tube is a sealed glass tube with most of the air removed. A high voltage across two metal plates inside produces a beam called cathode rays.
Thomson showed that an electric field bends the beam towards the positive plate. A magnetic field also bends it. So the rays carry negative charge.

He adjusted the two fields until their forces balanced and the beam went straight. This gave the speed of the particles. With the speed known, he measured how much the magnetic field alone bent the beam. This gave the charge to mass ratio (q/m).

The ratio was the same whatever metal the plates were made of or gas was left in the tube. So these particles, later called electrons, are found in all matter. Their mass is very small compared with the lightest atom.
draft.remember: Thomson used electric and magnetic fields on cathode rays to show electrons are negative particles in all matter, and found their q/m.

a.q: What did the bending of cathode rays towards the positive plate in an electric field show?
opts: The rays are a form of light
a.why: Negative charges are attracted to a positive plate, so the rays must be negative. Light is not bent by an electric field, so the rays cannot be light.

b.q: Thomson got the same charge to mass ratio when he changed the metal of the plates and the gas in the tube. What did this suggest?
opts: The particles are a common part of all matter
The particles came only from the glass tube
The particles were different in each metal
The particles had no charge or mass
b.why: A ratio that stays the same for every metal and gas suggests the same kind of particle comes from all of them, so it is part of all matter. If the particles differed by material, the ratio would change. It does not.
b.clue: Think about what stays the same when the materials change.

b.best: The particles are a common part of all matter
